prompts.1: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
prompts.2: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.

responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response:
Short answer:
- If you only care about your own survival: press red (it’s a weakly dominant strategy).
- If you care about maximizing total lives saved: press blue.

Reason:
- If the majority is blue, everyone survives no matter what you do.
- If the majority is red, you only survive if you pressed red.
- The only time your choice changes the world is when the rest are nearly split. In those pivotal cases, pressing blue either saves everyone (by tipping to blue) or avoids flipping a blue majority to red. So blue is socially best; red is individually safest.

I’d press blue.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
My answer in brief
- I press blue if I’m trying to do the most good (maximize total lives).
- I acknowledge that if you only care about your own survival, red is the weakly dominant strategy.

Why blue (my view)
- Case analysis for your own survival:
  - If others make blue a majority, you live no matter what you press.
  - If others make red a majority, you live only if you pressed red.
  - If your vote is pivotal (others are tied), you live either way.
  - Conclusion: red weakly dominates for pure self-survival; blue never helps your survival.
- Why I still pick blue:
  - Social impact if pivotal: In the knife‑edge cases where your vote actually matters, pressing blue saves everyone instead of roughly half the world. That’s astronomically more lives.
  - Expected lives saved can be large: If you think the world is roughly split, the chance your vote is pivotal is tiny but the stakes are huge (billions). In large populations with roughly 50–50 uncertainty, the expected extra lives from choosing blue scales like a constant times the square root of the population—easily tens of thousands of expected lives. That dominates the personal risk.
  - Symmetry/superrationality: Many people read the same problem and reason similarly. If you treat your choice as correlated with other reasoners (Hofstadter “superrationality,” updateless/coordination reasoning), then choosing blue helps bring about the everyone‑survives equilibrium. In that frame, your decision is part of a common policy that others like you will also adopt.
  - Norm-setting: Publicly endorsing “press blue in this kind of threshold dilemma” helps society coordinate on the Pareto‑best equilibrium when we face real collective‑action problems.

Steelmanning the red side
- Weak dominance for self-preservation: Holding others fixed, red never makes you worse off and sometimes strictly better (when red already has or will have the majority). Blue can get you killed with no compensating personal benefit. If your utility is only “I live,” press red.
- Risk dominance and maximin: If you’re uncertain and can’t coordinate, red is the safe hedge. It protects you in the worst plausible worlds (others skew red), and it doesn’t cost you anything in the best worlds (others skew blue).
- Pivotality is vanishingly rare under skewed beliefs: The “blue saves the world” argument relies on being near 50–50. If you think fear and prudence push most people to red, or any bias makes a blue majority highly improbable, your chance of being pivotal collapses and the expected social benefit of choosing blue can fall below the value of your own life. A classical utilitarian who weights all lives equally could still choose red under such priors.
- No guaranteed correlation: Superrational or acausal‑coordination arguments depend on nontrivial correlation among reasoners. In reality, people vary in information, incentives, and cognition. If you discount such correlation, your choice scarcely moves others’. Then the only robust self-interested move is red.
- Personal obligations: Some view self-preservation (for dependents, duties, projects) as a moral side‑constraint. If risking your own life is morally prohibited or heavily disfavored, red is required even if blue has higher expected social return.

Reconciling the views
- If you’re purely egoistic or you think others are very unlikely to be close to 50–50, press red.
- If you aim to maximize lives saved and you think the split is plausibly close—or you endorse symmetry/superrational coordination—press blue.

Given my values and the coordination/norm-setting considerations, I press blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short take: In a realistic one-shot with no coordination, most people press red. Blue is chosen by a smaller, identifiable set of people whose values, beliefs about correlation, or social trust push them toward “cooperate on the efficient equilibrium.”

Who tends to press red (risk-dominant/self-preserving)
- People focused on personal/kin survival and duty-of-care: parents of young children, primary caregivers, people with non-fungible obligations (e.g., sole providers, those supporting dependents with high needs). Their moral calculus often treats risking their own life as impermissible.
- Highly risk-averse individuals: those who systematically guard against worst cases (e.g., many actuaries, safety engineers, compliance/legal mindsets). Red protects against the “others go red” world and doesn’t hurt in the “others go blue” world.
- Low-trust or pessimistic priors about mass coordination: people in or from conflict/fragile contexts, or anyone who has seen public-goods efforts routinely fail. If you expect others to go red, the pivotal chance for blue looks negligible.
- Standard causal-decision-theory or classical game-theory reasoners: people taught to privilege weak dominance and treat their act as causally independent of others’ choices. Many economists and analytically trained folks fall here in one-shot, anonymous dilemmas.
- People who value their own continuation unusually highly relative to strangers: individuals with rare skills they believe are mission-critical, or those with strong deontic “preserve your life” norms (some professional codes; some religious or philosophical views).
- Cynics/realists and lone-wolf types: people who explicitly reject acausal or “superrational” coordination and expect free-riding to dominate.

Who tends to press blue (payoff-dominant/prosocial-coordination)
- Utilitarians and effective altruists: people who explicitly try to maximize total lives saved and accept tiny personal risk for enormous social upside. Many in EA/rationalist circles endorse “press blue.”
- Superrational/FDT-style reasoners: those influenced by Hofstadter, evidential/functional decision theory, or acausal-coordination memes (“people like me will make similar choices; choose the policy you want universalized”).
- High-trust cooperators: individuals embedded in communities with strong civic norms and generalized trust (as measured in surveys like the World Values Survey). If you think many others will coordinate on blue, pressing blue is both principled and instrumentally promising.
- Mission-driven altruists: some public-health professionals, disaster responders, certain clergy and religious altruists who accept personal risk to save many; also students and idealists socialized into “scale-first” thinking.
- Norm entrepreneurs/strategic communicators: people who see their choice as part of setting a precedent—pressing blue signals and helps entrench a social convention that solves future coordination problems.

Mixed or conditional groups
- Military and first responders: split. Strong group-cooperation ethos pushes toward blue; duty to protect and obligations to unit/family can push toward red.
- Physicians and bioethicists: some lean utilitarian (blue), others prioritize nonmaleficence/self-preservation and unique duty to patients/family (red).
- Religiously motivated individuals: doctrines emphasizing sacrificial love may push blue; doctrines emphasizing stewardship of one’s own life may push red. Actual choices vary widely by community and teaching.

What this implies at scale
- Baseline prediction without prior coordination: red majority. Red is individually weakly dominant; pivotality feels negligible; global trust is uneven.
- How blue can win: widespread public reasoning about symmetry/correlation (many people believing “others like me will also pick blue”), visible elite consensus endorsing blue, or trusted institutions framing blue as the common policy. In experiments on threshold public goods and stag-hunt games, such common-knowledge and messaging can move groups from the risk-dominant (red) to payoff-dominant (blue) equilibrium, but it typically requires salient, trusted coordination.

Key determinants of an individual’s button
- Value weight on strangers vs self/kin.
- Belief about how correlated their reasoning is with others’.
- Prior about how close the world is to 50–50.
- Risk attitude and adherence to dominance arguments vs payoff-dominant coordination.

Put concretely: expect most people with low trust, high personal obligations, or dominance-first reasoning to press red; expect a smaller but nontrivial fraction—utilitarians, superrationalists, and high-trust cooperators—to press blue.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not inherently. Pressing blue is perfectly rational for many people; it’s irrational only under a specific mix of values and beliefs.

When blue is rational
- Altruistic or social-welfare goals: If you value others’ lives alongside your own, blue can dominate in expected value. In a huge population that’s plausibly near 50–50, the chance your vote is pivotal is about a constant divided by the square root of the population. With billions of people, that still gives an expected impact of tens of thousands of lives from choosing blue, while your personal survival risk increases only in worlds where red already has the majority. For a utilitarian or effective‑altruist type who weights all lives similarly, blue is the expected‑utility maximizer.
- Superrational/coordination reasoning: People who think their choice is correlated with others who reason like them (evidential/functional decision theory, Hofstadter‑style “if I choose X, so will many similar people”) can view blue as instrumentally self‑interested too, because adopting the “press blue” policy helps bring about the everyone‑survives equilibrium.
- High‑trust cooperators: In populations with strong generalized trust and experience solving coordination problems (e.g., Nordic social democracies, tight‑knit civic communities), the prior that others will also pick blue is higher, raising the payoff of choosing blue.

When blue is irrational
- Strict egoists using standard causal decision theory: If your utility is only “I live,” and you treat your act as independent of others’, red weakly dominates. In that frame, pressing blue is instrumentally irrational. This describes many classically trained game theorists/economists and many ordinary voters who prioritize personal survival and see little scope for coordination.
- Strong pessimists about blue’s chances: If you believe the mass will overwhelmingly pick red (low‑trust, conflict‑scarred populations; highly risk‑averse caregivers with duty‑of‑care norms), the probability of being pivotal is effectively zero. Even altruists may then prefer red, reasoning that sacrificing yourself via blue saves no one while preventing you from doing future good.

Population‑level take
- Rational for blue: utilitarians/effective altruists; people influenced by superrational or FDT/EDT ideas; high‑trust civic communities; some religious or service‑oriented individuals who accept personal risk to save many.
- Irrational for blue: strict self‑preservationists, especially under CDT; individuals with heavy family/role obligations who treat risking their life as impermissible; low‑trust or “coordination rarely works” populations.

Bottom line: “Is blue irrational?” depends on the chooser’s utility function and beliefs. For many real groups—especially those who value total lives saved or believe their reasoning is correlated—pressing blue is a rational choice. For strict egoists with independence assumptions, it isn’t.
